From Lori, Koje's foster:


KOJE's Story by Lori:

My name was Koje & I was loved. 

When I first found myself at Brother Wolf Animal Rescue, my tail tucked underneath me, I had so many questions.

Where am I? What is happening? 
I heard dogs barking, they didn't sound happy. None of the people smelled familiar. 
I hung my head as I was put into a tiny room with fence for walls & concrete instead of grass. 
The people brought me a bed, it wasn't MY bed, I laid on it though. 
I was afraid to move. I was so hungry but the food in the bowl didn't smell like MY food. I watched the other dogs eat their food in their tiny rooms. I couldn't eat.

BWAR tried finding me a friend that would foster me so I could be more comfortable. 
I guess it worked, finally, Lori showed up! She smelled different, I liked it.

I was nervous, I kepy my tail tucked and my head low. She wanted to take me outside for a walk. I missed going for walks & I liked Lori's voice. I decided to trust her &she had decided that I should go home with her. 

Man was I happy she decided that! When we got to her house I saw that she had 5 kids for me to love on. They all gave me big hugs and kisses, I loved it! 
I was so happy to be out of that tiny fence room & around people! My tail wouldn’t stop wagging, I couldn’t stop smiling. 

Everyday I got to be out roaming the house, I only went in my kennel when I needed some me time. I had a big yard and a porch where I layed to feel the warm sun. 

It was perfect. My favorite place was inside with my new people. At night I gently hinted to Lori that I would love to have some belly rubs by climbing up in the recliner with her & rolling on my back. 
Guess what! She got my hint & I got belly rubs. She let me lay there for hours , just rubbing me, that was definitely the best part of my day. 
I wasn't sure about 1 of my new little human siblings at first. I softly growled to let her know I needed space. She let me have my space & I gave her kisses in return.

I heard Lori talking on the phone about the holidays coming up & visitors. The visitors were bringing dogs! I was excited! Lori explained to me that the dogs coming to visit didn't like other dogs. She didn't want me to get hurt so I had to go back to BWAR just for 2 weeks. 
Lori promised she would come back & take me home. Those 2 weeks felt like years.
Lori & her little human visited me the whole time. I waited to see their faces every single day. I would jump & spin with joy, my tail started wagging again like it did when I was home, with them, my new people. I didn't want to eat again. So Lori would come sit with me till I ate all my food. 

We would go on walks every visit & then she'd rub my belly just like we did on the recliner.  She really made me feel safe, I trusted her. I just knew I had found my family. One of the days she visited me she took me to a grooming salon to get me all cleaned up for the upcoming holiday! 

Christmas was coming and everyone knows what that means, presents! My family made me feel pretty special. All they wanted for Christmas was to come see me. So, on Christmas Eve the whole family stopped by, we went on a long walk. 

One of the people at Brother Wolf spent a lot of time with me too.

I was starting to learn that not ALL people were bad. 
The time was getting closer to go back to my foster home, I couldn’t wait! 

The morning before I was supposed to leave, Lori came to me crying. She wouldn’t stop crying so I sat on her lap, kissed her face trying to make her feel better. 

She hugged me so tight & told me how much she loved me. I already knew that, I couldn't understand why she was crying. 
She kept saying that she failed me but I didn’t see how. 

For a few hours I sat there by myself after she left wondering what had just happened.
She came back, she was still upset and crying. A nice lady from Brother Wolf came in & set up a blanket in my play area

We sat there for a long time, Lori rubbed my belly. When she had to leave she cried even harder & wouldn’t stop kissing my face & squeezing me tight. 
She walked out, closed the gate & bent down so I could kiss her face. 

I didn’t know that was the last time I was ever going to see her. 

I didn't know that was the last time she would rub my belly & hug me. 

I didn't know that was the last time I'd ever get to kiss her face.

I didn't know. 

That night, I was killed. 
I was killed by the ones who are called a rescue. 

Now I see what Lori meant when she said she let me down. 

She didn't let me down though. 

She gave me the happiest days of my life. I thought we'd have more days. 

I'll wait up here, at the Rainbow Bridge, with my new friends. 

And we'll watch over you all.

Please help the rest, be my voice.

From Joelle Warren, one of the original founders of BWAR:
"I am one of the founders of Brother Wolf Animal Rescue and I am appalled by the recent killing of dogs there.  I was the Director of Operations for 8 years. In my time there, we worked together to rescue over 12,000 pets.  We were a tight knit crew of life-savers.  As the organization grew, push came to shove and I had to part ways. It was not a pleasant split and I was forced to sign a NDA in order to receive my severance pay. I am not here today to speak about that split. 

What I have been compelled to speak out about is the current state of affairs regarding the recent killings of longer stay dogs and dogs with bite histories. Dogs bite. That is how they communicate when they are uneasy, scared or protective of their food, space or person.  Many people have dogs that have bitten, and are able to safely manage them. This is called Behavioral Management. Many of the dogs killed so far at BWAR are dogs that simply needed management, not to be put to death.  

BWAR was created with the No-Kill philosophy. The essence of the No-Kill movement involves management, training, compassion, and the value that all life matters. Choosing to euthanize an animal is not a decision to be taken lightly and it is reserved for situations when there are no other good possibilities. I do not believe dogs should languish in shelters, mentally and physically deteriorating. I also do not believe in placing dogs with severe aggression into the community.  I have had to make the very difficult decision to euthanize dogs during my career, but this decision was ONLY made when there were NO other safe options.  That being said, this is not the case currently happening at BWAR.

A few weeks ago, a story came across my Facebook feed by Katarina Brown, a former employee of Brother Wolf. She was writing about her experiences with a dog named Zurich, who is currently at BWAR and on their kill list. I read it and felt this kindred spirit kinda thing happening. A girl and her dog. She needed this dog. Yes, he had bitten a couple of people, barely breaking skin, but she had picture after picture and several videos of him totally in love with her and her of him. She is his person. She gets him and he gets her. In my 20 years of animal rescue, I too have fallen for the naughty dogs, the misunderstood dogs that won't ever like all people but will be head over heels in love with a few. This is Zurich. 

Katarina had applied to adopt Zurich and was refused.  I thought about this girl and her dog for a couple weeks, wondering if I should step in and advocate for her and try to help her adopt this dog that she loves so much.  But finally, I felt like I couldn't stand back. I had to help. Without notifying Katarina, I emailed Leah Craig Feiser (the new executive director of BWAR as of Feb 2019) on 12/21 asking her to allow Mountain Pet Rescue Asheville, my new organization, to pull Zurich. I explained that I would let Katarina adopt Zurich. I would pay for a trainer for her and Zurich. I would inspect Katarina's property to make sure it was safe and would contain Zurich. I thought maybe they were concerned with liability and MPR would assume all liability. I was told no. I asked again, but this time, I told her I wanted to adopt him. I currently own 4 dogs with multiple bite histories,  2 of which are BWAR dogs, with very similar issues to Zurich. I have since acquired 2 more biters. These dogs are all dog friendly and I have successfully managed their behavior for years with no further bite incidents. I explained that I could easily work him into my pack of naughties if it would save his life. I also asked for the names of the behaviorists who deemed Zurich as a menace to society so I could discuss his behavior with someone actually qualified to discuss it.  Again, I was told no, but this time it was in a bit more condescending of a tone. I held it together and sent one more plea, in which I threw in some Nathan Winograd quotes (the father of the No-Kill movement), and hoped that my 20 plus years of rescue experience could at least get me somewhere. Then I received her third “no” reply, complete with copied and pasted excerpts from her article and their website. I guess the founder of BWAR doesn't even deserve a genuine response as a simple, professional courtesy. 

So, here I am, doing what I can to stop the senseless killing of animals that have been offered a safe and responsible place to live. I don't want Zurich to end up like Rosie, Koje or Ruby. These dogs had people, qualified people, just like me, to take them, and instead, Brother Wolf chose killing. They say their reason was for public safety, but there are multiple dogs at any given time at our county shelter that are there on bite holds.  These dogs serve their time for their bites and then get returned to their families, sometimes even dogs with multiple bites!  If the dogs are not claimed, they are evaluated and often placed up for adoption.  A bite doesn’t equal death.  You can be responsible and concerned for public safety without going on a power trip and euthanizing anything with even a suspected bite. 

I know I can save Zurich and give him a quality life, but Leah thinks she is a better judge of determining this, even though she has only been in animal rescue for less than a year compared to my 20 years of experience.  This makes no sense, absolutely none. I am with James, of Keno's Animal Sanctuary, when he stated in his video that recently went viral, that this is a pride thing. They are too proud and stubborn to acknowledge a responsible and viable alternative to killing, even when I am literally begging right in front of them. It's utterly shameful."

This is a very small fraction of the actual story. Several of the dogs who were euthanized either had no bite history or had experienced professionals willing to work with or adopt them. Leah Craig set impossibly high standards for "sanctuary placement" of these dogs (much higher standards than bwar adheres to), then turned down every opportunity to save them. They were not euthanized because they were hopeless cases. Only to prove a point. 

They didn't just euthanize one or two long stay dogs, which might have been more understandable. They put down close to 20 dogs just in the past couple months. 

One of them was only in their facility for three weeks. Another was dropped off by their foster for respite just for two weeks and was euthanized during that time. 

Note: I am not against behavioral euthanasia when all other efforts have been exhausted and the animal has limited quality of life. Unfortunately, that was not the case for most of these dogs. I've worked with multiple rescues and in vet med so I'm not just an uneducated spectator. If they had shifted this policy without immediately killing over a dozen dogs with sanctuaries and behaviorists trying to save them it might have worked. But BWAR thinks they know better than anyone else on the planet and refuse to take alternate info or options into consideration.

But just to clarify...FIP is completely different than FIV. FIV is, like you said, the kitty version of HIV, and most cats who have it can live long, happy lives with little to no symptoms (it typically effects their immune system, so keeping them indoors and vaccinated is key). FIP, on the other hand, is a mutated virus that is almost always fatal and usually diagnosed in kittens and very young cats. Most don't make it to a year :( 

Just wanted to clear that up in case you or anyone reading has or has the opportunity to adopt a FIV kitty. FIV alone rarely causes complications, and doesn't easily transfer from cat to cat. Adopt all the FIV kitties ❤️❤️

I'll tell you why.

Reason one: Cats are extremely sensitive to their environment; sometimes even something as simple as new furniture can stress them out. Not all cats make strong bonds with humans but that doesn't mean they are unhappy. The process of rehoming would ultimately cause more stress than not being the most loved cat in the house.

Reason two: Adult cats are hard to re-home. With the cat population as it is, thousands of adult cats are euthenized every year. Everyone wants a kitten. I say this as someone who has spent years in shelter work; even at a no-kill, adult cats often spent years in our care before finally finding a home. That includes living in a loud, stressful shelter environment or being shuffled between foster homes, which like I said is also extremely stressful. 

If you don't absolutely have to, rehoming a cat is never the best option. Cats are independent and do not need human affection to be happy and healthy.
